Subfactors, index and finite-depth classification

A finite-index tunnel is enough

A finite-depth inclusion has a tunnel whose relative commutants generate a factor of finite index. The generating-tunnel argument can start from that conclusion itself. It does not need a finite principal graph. Two points require additional proofs: changing the tunnel must preserve factoriality of its closure, and finite matrix corners must still approximate a late relative commutant when the number of its blocks is unbounded.

We assume Going up and down the Jones tower, Reflected traces and a uniform bound along a tunnel, Detecting a generating tunnel, Matrix corners approximate a tunnel, and A generating tunnel and the classification theorem. We use one-step tunnel uniqueness, the skipped-level basic construction, the finite-basis theorem, the tracial ultrapower, and the finite-corner approximation property of the separable hyperfinite II₁ factor. Their precise prerequisites are the ones stated in those lessons. The arguments below replace every use of finite depth in passing from a finite-index tunnel to a generating one. References are [Jones] and [Popa].

This theorem supplies a criterion for generating tunnels. It does not assert that finite index of alone produces the extra finite-index closure in (29.1). Finite depth supplied that step in Theorem 16.4. At infinite depth the existence of such a closure is a substantive additional question.

Solution. In with uniform weights, the maximum is , while the sum of minimal weights is one. Lemma 16.1 bounds the removed trace by , so it is the sum that must vanish. The small-block projection and the factor hypothesis rule out this persistent scalar-block example.
